opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of people read the bitter lesson too narrowly. The usual takeaway is "don't hand-engineer anything, just scale compute and data, and general methods will win." That's true, but people then jump to a second conclusion that isn't in Sutton's essay: that the right general method is next-token prediction on text, and everything else, vision included, should just be tokenized and thrown into the same pipe.

My view is that language is itself a kind of human prior. It's an incredibly compressed, curated representation of the world that humans built over thousands of years. When we train only on language, we're benefiting from all that human engineering. In a sense that's the opposite of the bitter lesson. It works great, but it means the model inherits our abstractions rather than discovering its own.

The visual world, the physical world, is different. There's no dictionary for pixels. The signal is continuous, high-dimensional, mostly redundant, and the important structure is hidden. So the question becomes: what's the right latent space to learn in? If you just predict raw pixels, you waste enormous capacity on texture and noise that don't matter. If you hand-design the latent space, you violate the bitter lesson. The interesting middle ground is learning latent representations that are themselves the product of scale. That's why I've been excited about things like representation alignment for diffusion models and building generative models on top of strong self-supervised encoders rather than plain VAEs.

So I'd frame it this way: the bitter lesson doesn't say "use language." It says use methods that scale with computation. For vision and world modeling, that means learning good latent spaces from raw sensory data, at scale, rather than borrowing language as a shortcut. Language models have shown us how far you can get by standing on humanity's shoulders. The next step is building systems that form their own representations of the world, and I think latent representations beyond language are where that happens. It's harder, it's less mature, but I think it's where the bitter lesson actually points.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning latent spaces from sensory data, but does not say those representations can be interpreted indirectly.

r002.rationale: It contrasts language’s inherited abstractions with systems that form their own representations from raw sensory data, describing latent representations beyond language.

r003.rationale: It says language models inherit human abstractions from language, which makes language training “the opposite of the bitter lesson” and limits discovery of their own representations.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the bitter lesson is often misread. People hear it as "stop designing things, just scale," but what Sutton actually said is that general methods that scale with compute beat hand-crafted human knowledge. The question is always: what is the general method? For language, the answer was almost given to us. Text is already a discrete, compressed, human-made representation. Tokens are a gift. You can pour compute into next-token prediction and the structure is already there.

Vision and the physical world don't come with that gift. Pixels are not a representation, they're a measurement. There's an enormous amount of redundancy, and most of it has nothing to do with what you'd want a model to understand. So when people say "just scale the pixel model," I think they're being faithful to the slogan but not to the lesson. Scaling raw pixel prediction spends most of your compute reconstructing texture and noise that no downstream task cares about.

That's where latent representations come in. I see learning a good latent space, something like what a self-supervised encoder gives you, as the vision analogue of what tokenization did for language. It's not injecting human priors about objects or parts. It's finding the right level of abstraction so that scaling becomes efficient. In our work on diffusion transformers, we saw this very clearly: when the latent space the generative model lives in is semantically richer, the model trains dramatically faster and the scaling curve looks healthier. The representation and the generation are not separate problems.

So my view is that latents are not a violation of the bitter lesson, they're a prerequisite for applying it outside language. The lesson says don't hard-code what the world looks like. It doesn't say the input space is sacred. Choosing to learn a compressed, meaningful space from data, and then scaling on top of it, is exactly the kind of general method the lesson favors. The mistake would be to freeze that space by hand. The right move is to let it be learned too, and to let it improve as compute grows.

The open question I'm still wrestling with is how unified this should be. Should the latent space for understanding and the one for generation be the same? Should it be shared across modalities? My instinct is yes, eventually, but right now we're still figuring out what the "token" of the visual world even is. That's the real frontier.

r001.rationale: The response describes learned latent spaces as compressed and semantically richer, but does not state that they can be interpreted indirectly.

r002.rationale: It contrasts visual latents with language tokens, but does not clearly state that nonlinguistic latent representations are unconstrained by language structure.

r003.rationale: The response calls text tokens a useful representation and contrasts language with vision, but does not attribute LLMs’ insufficient adherence to the bitter lesson to language constraints.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether language is the right representation for everything. Language is incredibly powerful, but it’s also a compressed description of our experience. When you describe a scene, you leave out a huge amount of information—its geometry, motion, all the details that are hard to put into words. So there’s no obvious reason that an intelligent system should have to translate everything into language before it can reason about it.

To me, learning latent representations outside language is very consistent with the bitter lesson. Instead of deciding ahead of time what concepts the model should use, you let those representations emerge from data and computation. The model might discover something useful that doesn’t correspond neatly to a word or a human-defined category.

But there’s a tension here. If we build a very elaborate system with handcrafted components for every kind of perception or reasoning, we might be moving against that lesson. The important distinction is between designing a learning mechanism and prescribing what it must learn. We still need architectures and objectives; the question is whether they enable learning at scale or impose a ceiling on it.

And I wouldn’t assume that a latent representation is better just because it’s not language. You have to demonstrate that it learns effectively, improves with more compute and data, and transfers to useful tasks. That’s where the bitter lesson becomes an empirical question: which approach keeps getting better as we scale it?

r001.rationale: The response says nonlinguistic representations can emerge and need not map neatly to words, but does not state that they can be interpreted indirectly.

r002.rationale: It says intelligent systems need not translate everything into language and that useful representations may not correspond to words or human-defined categories, conveying that they are not confined to language’s structure.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute LLMs’ failure to follow the bitter lesson to constraints imposed by language.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the bitter lesson is about which approaches continue to improve as you give them more data and more compute. It doesn’t necessarily tell us that language is the right representation for everything.

Language is a powerful interface, but it’s also a compressed description of the world. If you describe a scene, you leave out an enormous amount of information: geometry, motion, physical interactions. So I wouldn’t assume that all intelligence should pass through language tokens. There may be representations learned directly from images, video, or actions that are much better suited to those things.

The important distinction is whether we hand-design those representations or let them emerge through learning. If we prescribe exactly what a visual representation should contain, we risk repeating the approaches the bitter lesson warns about. But learning a latent space from large amounts of data is very much consistent with that lesson.

Of course, saying ‘latent representation’ doesn’t solve the problem. What’s the learning objective? What prevents the representation from discarding information you’ll need later? Can you scale it effectively? Those are the real questions. I’d treat language as one very useful part of the system, while leaving room for the system to learn other ways of representing the world.

r001.rationale: The response proposes learning representations directly from images, video, or actions, but does not say they can be interpreted indirectly.

r002.rationale: It says intelligence need not pass through language tokens, but does not clearly state that nonlinguistic latent representations are unconstrained by language structure.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute LLMs’ insufficient adherence to the bitter lesson to constraints imposed by language.
